name: AWS - IAM Permission Scoping with Compromised Credentials
command:
aws --profile <profile> iam list-user-policies --user-name <username>
aws --profile <profile> iam list-attached-user-policies --user-name <username>
aws --profile <profile> iam list-groups-for-user --user-name <username>
aws --profile <profile> iam list-attached-group-policies --group-name <groupname>
aws --profile <profile> iam get-policy-version --policy-arn <arn> --version-id <version>
description: Map the exact IAM permissions of a compromised AWS identity. Start with sts get-caller-identity to get the username/role name, then enumerate: (1) inline user policies, (2) managed policies attached directly to the user, (3) groups the user belongs to, (4) group-attached policies, (5) get the policy document for each policy version to read the actual Allow/Deny statements. This maps the attack surface — what services and actions are available with these credentials.
source: OSCP PEN-200 Chapter 24: Enumerating AWS Cloud Infrastructure (24.4.3)

examples.label: Step 1 - Identify the compromised user from STS
examples.command:
aws --profile target sts get-caller-identity
# Arn: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:user/support/clouddesk-plove -> username = clouddesk-plove

examples.label: Step 2 - Check inline policies on the user
Step 3 - Check managed policies attached to the user
Step 4 - Find what groups the user belongs to
Step 5 - List inline policies on the group
Step 6 - List managed policies attached to the group
Step 7 - Find the current version of a managed policy
examples.command:
aws --profile target iam list-policy-versions --policy-arn "arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/job-function/SupportUser"
# Look for IsDefaultVersion: true -> that's the active version

examples.label: Step 8 - Read the actual policy document (what is allowed/denied)
Step 9 - Check what IAM read permissions are available

notes: IAM permissions can come from: (1) inline user policy, (2) managed policy directly attached to user, (3) group membership -> group inline or managed policies, (4) resource-based policies on services (S3, Lambda, etc.), (5) permission boundaries. Permission boundaries RESTRICT the maximum effective permissions — a boundary that allows only S3 means even if a policy grants EC2 access, the user cannot use EC2. Explicit Deny always overrides Allow regardless of source. AWS-managed policies (arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/) can be read via get-policy-version even by the subject user — they are public. Customer-managed policies (arn:aws:iam::<account_id>:policy/) require iam:GetPolicyVersion which may not be granted. Workaround: use get-account-authorization-details (see aws-iam-full-dump) if broader read permissions exist.

references.title: OffSec PEN-200 - Enumerating AWS Cloud Infrastructure

recommended.note: Run sts get-caller-identity first to get the username for subsequent commands.
If iam:Get*/List* permissions are available, use get-account-authorization-details for a full IAM dump.
Pacu iam__enum_permissions automates this permission enumeration.

defense.why_it_works: After initial IAM enumeration, scoping determines the specific permissions of the current credential — what actions the attacker can actually perform. aws iam simulate-principal-policy, enumerate-iam (tool), or checking attached policies reveals which services and actions are allowed. This avoids triggering alerts from calling unauthorized APIs and identifies the exact privilege escalation path available (e.g., has iam:CreatePolicyVersion but not iam:CreateUser — can escalate via policy version).
defense.prerequisites: AWS credentials with at least iam:GetUser and iam:ListAttachedUserPolicies. AWS CLI. enumerate-iam tool (or manual policy inspection). Understanding of IAM escalation paths.
defense.impact: T1087.004 Account Discovery: Cloud Account + T1069.003 Permission Groups Discovery: Cloud Groups. Identifies exact permissions of the current credential — maps specific privilege escalation paths, determines which resources are accessible, and prioritizes attack actions.
defense.detection:
CloudTrail: iam:SimulatePrincipalPolicy is an unusual API call that developers rarely make — highly suspicious. iam:GetUser + iam:ListAttachedUserPolicies + iam:GetPolicyVersion sequence from a single principal. enumerate-iam generates many parallel API calls that appear as high-volume errors in CloudTrail.
Processes performing local or domain account enumeration by invoking account directory queries or security APIs followed by structured output of account lists (DET0587/AN1612).
Suspicious shell commands or unauthorized access to /etc/passwd or /etc/shadow (AN1613).
Directory service queries or system utilities accessing account metadata stores, producing enumeration output (AN1614).
Cloud provider API calls where principals retrieve IAM users or roles in rapid succession (AN1615).
ESXi host account configuration or management APIs queried to retrieve user account listings (AN1617).
defense.artifacts: CloudTrail: iam:SimulatePrincipalPolicy call | CloudTrail: high-volume failed API calls from enumerate-iam (AccessDenied errors) | GuardDuty: 'Discovery:IAMUser/AnomalousBehavior'
defense.prevention:
Same as IAM enumeration: least-privilege policies, CloudTrail alerting. Specifically alert on iam:SimulatePrincipalPolicy calls — rare in production, common in attacker enumeration. Use IAM Access Analyzer to proactively identify over-permissioned resources before attackers find them.
Operating System Configuration: Prevent administrator account enumeration via UAC (GPO: HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\CredUI\EnumerateAdministrators).
User Account Management: Manage creation, modification, use, and permissions associated with user accounts.
defense.evasion: Use iam:SimulatePrincipalPolicy sparingly or not at all. Manually read attached policy documents instead of simulate (generates fewer suspicious API calls). Infer permissions from successful API calls rather than explicit simulation.
defense.misconfiguration: No alerting on iam:SimulatePrincipalPolicy. No CloudTrail enabled in all regions. IAM policies not reviewed for escalation paths (iam:PassRole, iam:CreatePolicyVersion, iam:AttachUserPolicy are common escalation primitives).
defense.vulnerable_config:
# IAM escalation path example — has PassRole + CreateFunction:
# Attacker finds:
# aws iam get-user-policy → allows lambda:CreateFunction + iam:PassRole
# → Can create Lambda with admin role → PrivEsc to admin

# IAM Access Analyzer not enabled:
aws accessanalyzer list-analyzers
# → No analyzers = no proactive permission review
defense.secure_config:
# Enable IAM Access Analyzer:
aws accessanalyzer create-analyzer --analyzer-name account-analyzer --type ACCOUNT
# → Identifies external access and cross-account resource sharing

# CloudTrail alert on SimulatePrincipalPolicy:
# CloudWatch metric filter:
# { $.eventName = 'SimulatePrincipalPolicy' }
# Alarm: any occurrence → immediate SNS alert

# Review escalation paths with Cloudsplaining:
# pip install cloudsplaining
# aws iam get-account-authorization-details > iam-full.json
# cloudsplaining scan --input iam-full.json --output report/
# → Identifies dangerous permission combinations
